questions.q: What is the difference between object/field-level security and record-level sharing?
options: They are two names for the exact same mechanism
Object/field-level security governs whether a user can act on an object or field at all; record-level sharing governs which specific records they can see or touch
Record-level sharing controls profiles, while object-level security controls OWD
Object-level security only applies to custom objects, never standard ones
questions.explain: A user can have full edit permission on an object (via profile/permission set) and still be unable to see a specific record with no sharing access — both layers have to say yes before a user can actually act on a record.

questions.q: Which record-access layer serves as the baseline "floor" that every other layer builds on top of?
options: Manual sharing
Sharing rules
Organization-wide defaults (OWD)
Role hierarchy
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline per object, from Private up to Public Read/Write, and every other layer (role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual sharing) can only add access on top of that floor.

questions.q: What does the role hierarchy layer do, by default, regarding record visibility?
options: It restricts every user's visibility to only their own records
It opens access upward: a user's manager and those above them can generally see and edit records owned by people below them
It replaces the need for OWD entirely
It only applies to custom objects, never standard objects
questions.explain: The role hierarchy models a management structure's natural need for visibility — a manager and everyone above them in the hierarchy automatically see records owned by people below them, without a separate grant.

questions.q: According to the additive-access rule, what happens if a user's profile/permission sets grant them edit access to an object but OWD for that object is Private and no sharing rule applies to them?
options: Sharing rules automatically override OWD in every case
The user cannot see or edit records they don't own and aren't shared on, because OWD is the layer that actually restricts access and nothing has widened it for this user
The user automatically gets Public Read/Write regardless of OWD
Object-level permissions always override record-level restrictions
questions.explain: Sharing rules and the role hierarchy can only widen access beyond OWD, never restrict it. With a restrictive Private OWD and no applicable sharing or hierarchy access, the user still can't see records they don't own, regardless of their object-level permission.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as a common design smell regarding sharing rules?
options: Using sharing rules at all, under any circumstances
An org with dozens of broad, overlapping sharing rules, usually meaning OWD was set more permissively than the data warranted and sharing rules are doing cleanup work they weren't meant to do
Setting OWD to Private for every single object without exception
Using the role hierarchy for vertical visibility
questions.explain: Sharing rules are meant to be a targeted exception for specific cross-team visibility, not the default access-control tool. Heavy reliance on many broad sharing rules usually signals OWD was set too permissively in the first place.
